sub: The Eucharistic celebration of the Roman Rite: its meaning, its parts and how to take part
sec: What the word means

“Mass” comes from the Latin words of dismissal, “Ite, missa est” (“Go, it is the sending”). The name reminds us that the Eucharist ends in mission: we are sent out to live what we have celebrated. The Mass is also called the Eucharist (thanksgiving), the Holy Sacrifice, the Lord's Supper and Holy Communion (CCC 1328–1332).

At every Mass the one sacrifice of Christ on the Cross is made present; bread and wine become his Body and Blood; and the faithful are fed with him. It is “the source and summit of the Christian life” (Lumen Gentium 11).
Its roots

The Roman Rite goes back to the liturgy of the Church of Rome. Its oldest Eucharistic Prayer, the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I), was substantially fixed by the sixth century. After the Second Vatican Council the Missal was renewed (1970), and the present English translation dates from 2011; in India the Mass is celebrated in many languages, including Malayalam, Tamil, Hindi and English.

Already in the second century St Justin Martyr described the Sunday celebration: readings from the apostles and prophets, a homily, prayers, the bringing of bread and wine, the great thanksgiving, the “Amen” of the people and Communion (First Apology 65–67). The shape of the Mass is that old.
How it unfolds
1. Introductory Rites. Entrance chant, sign of the Cross and greeting; the Penitential Act; the Kyrie; the Gloria on Sundays (outside Advent and Lent) and feasts; the Collect.

2. Liturgy of the Word. The First Reading (usually from the Old Testament), the Responsorial Psalm, the Second Reading on Sundays, the Gospel Acclamation and the Gospel, the homily, the Creed on Sundays and solemnities, and the Universal Prayer (Prayer of the Faithful).

3. Liturgy of the Eucharist. The preparation of the gifts; the Eucharistic Prayer with its Preface and Sanctus, the Epiclesis over the gifts, the Institution Narrative and Consecration, the Anamnesis (memorial) and offering, the intercessions, and the final Doxology answered by the great “Amen”.

4. Communion Rite and Concluding Rites. The Lord's Prayer, the Sign of Peace, the Lamb of God with the breaking of the bread, Holy Communion, the prayer after Communion; then the blessing and the dismissal: “Go forth, the Mass is ended.”
What the Church believes
The Mass is a true sacrifice, the memorial of Christ's Passover, making present the sacrifice of the Cross (CCC 1362–1367).

By the consecration the whole substance of bread and wine is changed into the Body and Blood of Christ: transubstantiation. Christ is present whole and entire under each species and in each part (CCC 1374–1377).
The priest acts in the person of Christ the Head; the whole assembly offers the sacrifice through the priest and with him (CCC 1348, 1368).
The Eucharist makes the Church: it unites us with Christ and with one another, commits us to the poor, and is the pledge of future glory (CCC 1396–1405).
How to take part well
Arrive in time; observe silence before Mass; take part with full, conscious and active participation (Sacrosanctum Concilium 14): listening, responding, singing, and offering yourself with Christ.

Observe the Eucharistic fast of one hour before Communion (water and medicine excepted; Code of Canon Law c. 919). Receive Communion reverently, in the manner approved in your diocese; say “Amen” to “The Body of Christ” as a confession of faith.
The altar and what surrounds it

The altar is the center of the church: it is both the altar of the sacrifice and the table of the Lord, and it stands for Christ himself (CCC 1182, 1383). It is kissed by the priest at the beginning and end of Mass and often contains relics of the saints. Near it stand the crucifix and candles.

The ambo is the table of the Word, from which the readings are proclaimed. The tabernacle, marked by a burning lamp, keeps the Blessed Sacrament for the sick and for adoration; we genuflect before it. The baptismal font, the presider's chair and the confessional complete the picture: every part of the church speaks of a sacrament.
Vessels, vestments and gestures

The chalice holds the wine and the paten the bread; the ciborium holds the consecrated hosts; the corporal, a square white linen, is spread on the altar under them; the purificator is used to wipe the chalice. All are treated with reverence because of what they hold.

The priest wears the alb (white garment of the baptized), the cincture, the stole (sign of priestly office) and the chasuble in the color of the day; the deacon wears the stole across the shoulder and the dalmatic. The faithful express their part with their bodies: standing for the Gospel and the prayers, sitting to listen, kneeling or bowing at the consecration according to the norms of their country, striking the breast, offering the sign of peace.
Questions people ask

May I receive Communion in the hand? Communion on the tongue is always permitted; Communion in the hand is permitted where the conference of bishops allows it, provided it is received with reverence and consumed at once. Follow the norms of your diocese.
How often may I receive? Every day if you are properly disposed; a second time on the same day only within a Mass in which you take part (c. 917), and as Viaticum in danger of death.
Why are some words still in Latin or Greek? “Amen”, “Alleluia”, “Hosanna” and “Kyrie eleison” come from the earliest Church; they remind us that we pray with Christians of every age and language.
What is Eucharistic adoration? Prayer before the Blessed Sacrament, exposed or in the tabernacle. It flows from the Mass and leads back to it (CCC 1378–1380).
notes: Anyone conscious of grave sin must not receive Holy Communion without first making a sacramental confession, except for a grave reason when confession is impossible, with an act of perfect contrition and the intention to confess as soon as possible (Code of Canon Law c. 916; CCC 1385).
The faithful are obliged to participate in Mass on Sundays and holy days of obligation; deliberately failing to do so without a serious reason is a grave sin (CCC 2181).
The liturgy may not be changed by any priest or group on their own authority (Sacrosanctum Concilium 22; Redemptionis Sacramentum).
Catholics may not receive Communion in non-Catholic celebrations except in the cases foreseen by Church law (CCC 1398–1401).
Show reverence to the Blessed Sacrament: genuflect before the tabernacle, dress modestly, keep silence in church.
Reverence for the Blessed Sacrament is shown by genuflecting before the tabernacle, keeping silence in the church and dressing with dignity.

sub: Advent, Christmas, Lent, the Triduum, Easter and Ordinary Time: how the Roman Rite unfolds the mystery of Christ
sec: The year of the Lord

In the Roman Rite the liturgical year begins with the First Sunday of Advent and ends with the Solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe. Within one year the Church celebrates the whole mystery of Christ: his coming, birth and manifestation, his public life, his Passion, death and Resurrection, his Ascension, the gift of the Spirit and the hope of his return in glory (CCC 1163–1171; General Norms for the Liturgical Year 1, 17).

The year does not merely recall past events. In each celebration the saving deeds of Christ are made present, so that the faithful may lay hold of them and be filled with saving grace (Sacrosanctum Concilium 102).
Sunday and the Easter Triduum

Sunday is the primordial feast day, the weekly Easter, the day the Lord rose (CCC 2174–2177). Only solemnities and feasts of the Lord may replace the Sunday of Ordinary Time; the Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter yield to no other celebration.

The summit of the whole year is the Easter Triduum: it begins with the evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, reaches its center in the celebration of the Lord's Passion on Good Friday and the Easter Vigil in the holy night, and closes with Evening Prayer of Easter Sunday. These are not three separate feasts but one celebration of the Paschal Mystery.
Advent

Advent has four Sundays and two characters. Until 16 December it turns our eyes to Christ's second coming at the end of time; from 17 to 24 December it prepares directly for the celebration of his birth, with the great O Antiphons (O Wisdom, O Lord, O Root of Jesse, O Key of David, O Dayspring, O King of the nations, O Emmanuel).

It is a season of joyful and devout expectation, not of penance in the strict sense. The Gloria is omitted so that it may sound new at Christmas. The Third Sunday is Gaudete Sunday (“Rejoice”), when rose vestments may be worn. The figures of Advent are Isaiah, John the Baptist and above all Mary, who waited for the Lord.
Christmas Time

Christmas Time runs from Evening Prayer I of the Nativity (24 December) to the Sunday after Epiphany, the Feast of the Baptism of the Lord. It includes the Octave of Christmas, the Feast of the Holy Family (the Sunday within the Octave, or 30 December), the Solemnity of Mary, Mother of God (1 January) and the Epiphany, the manifestation of Christ to the nations.

The Nativity has four Masses: the Vigil, the Mass during the Night, at Dawn and during the Day. In many countries, including India, the Epiphany is celebrated on the Sunday between 2 and 8 January; follow your diocesan calendar.
Lent and Holy Week

Lent begins on Ash Wednesday and lasts until the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday. It has a twofold character: it prepares catechumens for Baptism and calls the faithful to repentance and to the renewal of their baptismal promises at Easter (Sacrosanctum Concilium 109). Its works are prayer, fasting and almsgiving (Matthew 6:1–18). The Gloria and the Alleluia are not sung.

The Fourth Sunday is Laetare Sunday, when rose may be worn. The Fifth Sunday points directly to the Passion. Holy Week begins with Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord, with the procession commemorating his entry into Jerusalem and the reading of the Passion. On the morning of Holy Thursday (or another day near it) the bishop celebrates the Chrism Mass with his priests, blessing the holy oils.
Easter Time

The fifty days from Easter Sunday to Pentecost are celebrated in joy as one feast, “one great Sunday” (General Norms 22). The first eight days form the Octave of Easter, each a solemnity; the Second Sunday of Easter is also called Divine Mercy Sunday.

The Ascension of the Lord falls on the fortieth day; in many countries, including India, it is moved to the following Sunday. The season closes with Pentecost, the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Easter candle burns at every liturgy throughout these fifty days and afterwards stands near the font and is lit at Baptisms and funerals.
Ordinary Time

Ordinary Time is not “ordinary” in the sense of dull: the word comes from the numbered (ordinal) weeks. In thirty-three or thirty-four weeks, in two parts (after Christmas Time and after Pentecost), the Church walks with Christ through his public life and teaching.

Within it fall great solemnities: the Most Holy Trinity, the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ, the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus, the Assumption of Mary (15 August), All Saints (1 November) and, on the last Sunday, Christ the King. November, with All Souls (2 November), turns our thoughts to the last things.
Colors, ranks and readings

Liturgical colors speak to the eye: violet for Advent and Lent; white (or gold) for Christmas and Easter Time, feasts of the Lord other than his Passion, of Mary, the angels and saints who were not martyrs; red for Palm Sunday, Good Friday, Pentecost, the apostles and martyrs; green for Ordinary Time; rose may be used on Gaudete and Laetare Sundays; black may be used at funerals and on All Souls.

Celebrations are ranked as solemnities, feasts and memorials (obligatory or optional), so that the mysteries of Christ keep the first place. Sunday readings follow a three-year cycle (Year A: Matthew; B: Mark; C: Luke; John in Lent, Easter Time and parts of Year B). Weekday first readings follow a two-year cycle (I in odd years, II in even years). The year that begins on 29 November 2026 is Year B for Sundays and Year I for weekdays.
notes: Ash Wednesday and Good Friday are days of fasting and abstinence. The law of fasting binds those who have completed their eighteenth year until the beginning of their sixtieth; the law of abstinence from meat binds those who have completed their fourteenth year (Code of Canon Law cc. 1251–1252).

All Fridays of the year and the whole season of Lent are penitential days and times; the conference of bishops determines how Friday penance is kept (cc. 1249–1253). Follow the norms of the Conference of Catholic Bishops of India (CCBI) or of your country.
Every Catholic must receive Holy Communion at least once a year, during Easter Time if possible, and confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042; c. 920, c. 989).

Holy days of obligation are determined for each country by the conference of bishops; in India follow the CCBI calendar and your diocese. On these days, as on Sundays, participation in Mass is a grave duty (c. 1247).
Pastors and parents should form children in a sense of penance even before they are bound by law (c. 1252).
Fasting must never endanger health; the sick, pregnant and nursing mothers and those doing heavy work are excused or should consult a priest (cf. CCC 2043).

sub: Why we confess, how to examine our conscience, how to make a good confession, and what the Church asks of us
sec: Christ gave this sacrament

On the evening of Easter the risen Lord breathed on the apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). Through the bishops and priests, their successors, Christ continues to forgive sins in the Church (CCC 1441–1445).

This sacrament has many names: conversion, penance, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation (CCC 1423–1424). In Kerala we usually say “Kumbasaram”. It is the sacrament of the prodigal son coming home and of the Father who runs to embrace him (Luke 15:20).
Why confess to a priest?

Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). But God chose to forgive through his Church: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive and to retain, which they could not use without hearing the sins (CCC 1461–1462). The priest is not a judge who condemns but a minister of mercy who acts in the person of Christ, the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep (CCC 1465).

Sin is never purely private. It wounds the Body of Christ, the Church. So reconciliation with God is also reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445, 1469). Hearing the words of absolution spoken aloud gives a certainty of forgiveness that our feelings alone cannot give.
Mortal and venial sin

Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart: it is a sin whose object is grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments. Mortal sin, unless repented and forgiven, separates us from God for ever (CCC 1861).

Venial sin weakens charity but does not destroy it (CCC 1862–1863). Confessing everyday faults is strongly recommended: it helps us form our conscience, fight evil tendencies, let ourselves be healed by Christ and grow in the life of the Spirit (CCC 1458).
Examining the conscience

An honest examination is the first step. Some questions, following the Commandments: Do I pray daily? Have I denied my faith or been ashamed of it? Have I used God's name carelessly or sworn falsely? Have I missed the Holy Qurbana or Mass on Sundays and days of obligation without serious reason?

Have I honored my parents and cared for them? Have I been unjust, violent or harsh at home, at work, with servants or employees? Have I harmed life: by anger, hatred, abortion, abuse of alcohol or drugs, reckless driving? Have I sinned against chastity in thought, word or deed, alone or with others, through pornography? Have I been faithful in marriage?

Have I stolen, cheated, taken bribes, failed to pay just wages or debts, wasted money while others are in need? Have I lied, gossiped, ruined another's good name, posted harmful things on social media? Have I been envious, greedy, proud, lazy in my duties? Have I neglected the poor?

Children and young people can ask more simply: Did I pray? Did I obey my parents and teachers? Did I tell lies, fight, use bad words, take what is not mine, cheat in exams, waste time on the phone, hurt anyone?
The three acts of the penitent

1. Contrition: sorrow of soul and hatred for the sin committed, with the resolution not to sin again. Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect contrition (attrition) comes from fear of punishment or the ugliness of sin, and is sufficient for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

2. Confession: telling the priest all mortal sins of which, after careful examination, we are conscious, with their kind and number, as far as we can (CCC 1456). Speak simply and honestly; there is no need for long stories or for naming other people.

3. Satisfaction: doing the penance the priest gives, to repair the harm and restore our habits as disciples of Christ (CCC 1459–1460). Where we have harmed others, we must also make it right: return what was taken, restore a damaged reputation, ask forgiveness.
How to make a good confession
Before: pray to the Holy Spirit for light; examine your conscience; awaken sorrow by looking at the crucifix and remembering God's love.

In the confessional: make the sign of the Cross; say how long it has been since your last confession and, if helpful, your state of life (married, student, priest or religious); confess your sins; listen to the priest's counsel and accept the penance; pray an act of contrition; receive absolution with faith. In the Eastern Churches the prayer of absolution often asks God to forgive the penitent; in the Latin Church the priest says “I absolve you”. Both are true and valid forms of the same sacrament.

A traditional act of contrition: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you, and I detest all my sins because of your just punishments, but most of all because they offend you, my God, who are all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of your grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. (Any approved act of contrition may be used, such as the one taught in your parish catechism.)
After: thank God; do the penance soon; repair any harm done; avoid the occasions of sin; come back regularly, not only when burdened by grave sin.
What the sacrament gives

Reconciliation with God, by which grace is restored; reconciliation with the Church; remission of the eternal punishment due to mortal sin and, at least in part, of temporal punishment; peace and serenity of conscience and spiritual consolation; and an increase of strength for the Christian battle (CCC 1468–1470, 1496).

Many people find that the hardest step is the first one, the walk to the confessional. Beyond it is the joy of the Father: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).
Children, first confession and frequent confession

Children who have reached the age of discretion (around seven) are prepared for their first confession before their first Holy Communion (CCC 1457; c. 914). Parents should go with them and confess themselves; children learn most from what they see.

The saints recommend confessing regularly, for example monthly, and before the great feasts. Many parishes offer confession during the Twenty-Five Days' Fast and the Great Fast or Lent; make use of these times.
notes: Every Catholic who has reached the age of discretion must confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042, 1457).

One who is conscious of mortal sin must not receive Holy Communion without first going to confession, except when there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess; then an act of perfect contrition must be made, with the intention of confessing as soon as possible (CCC 1457, 1385).

Deliberately hiding a mortal sin in confession makes the confession invalid and adds the sin of sacrilege; the hidden sin and the sacrilege must be confessed. Forgetting a sin is not hiding it: the forgotten sin is forgiven and should be mentioned at the next confession.
The priest is bound by the absolute seal of confession: he may never reveal or use what he hears, under the most severe penalties (CCC 1467; Code of Canon Law c. 983; CCEO c. 733).
Absolution requires real contrition and the purpose of amendment; it cannot be given to one who refuses to give up a grave sin or to repair a grave injustice.

General absolution without individual confession is allowed only in grave necessity (danger of death, or very large numbers with no possibility of individual confession for a long time); grave sins must then be confessed individually as soon as possible (CCC 1483).
Some very grave sins carry penalties whose remission is reserved; if this concerns you, speak to a priest, who will explain the path of reconciliation.

sub: How we are born into Christ, sealed with the Spirit and brought to the table of the Lord
sec: Christ commands it

Before his Ascension the risen Lord sent the apostles: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). On the day of Pentecost Peter told the crowd: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ so that your sins may be forgiven; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

Baptism is the door of the Christian life and of the other sacraments (CCC 1213). It is called the bath of new birth (Titus 3:5) and enlightenment (Hebrews 6:4): “no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit” (John 3:5).
How Baptism is celebrated

In the Rite of Baptism for Children the family is welcomed at the door of the church and asked what name they have chosen and what they ask of the Church; the child is signed with the Cross. The Word of God is proclaimed, followed by intercessions and the litany of the saints. There is a prayer of exorcism and an anointing with the oil of catechumens.

At the font the water is blessed; the parents and godparents renounce sin and profess the faith. The priest or deacon baptizes by immersion or by pouring water three times, saying: “N., I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” The child is anointed on the crown of the head with Chrism, clothed in a white garment and given a candle lit from the Easter candle; the Ephphetha may be prayed over the ears and mouth.

Adults are received through the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults: a catechumenate with stages and rites, ending usually at the Easter Vigil with Baptism, Confirmation and First Communion together.
Confirmation in the Latin Church

In the Latin Church Confirmation is usually given at a later age (the age of discretion or as fixed by the bishops' conference), so that the young person can receive it consciously. The ordinary minister is the bishop, who may delegate a priest (CCC 1312–1313).

The essential rite is the anointing with Chrism on the forehead, with the laying on of the hand and the words: “Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1300). Candidates renew their baptismal promises and choose a sponsor, ideally one of their baptismal godparents.
What Baptism does

Baptism forgives original sin and all personal sins, with all punishment due to sin (CCC 1263). It makes us a new creation, adopted children of God, members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265). It joins us to the Church, the Body of Christ (CCC 1267).

It marks the soul with an indelible spiritual seal, which no sin can erase; therefore Baptism is never repeated (CCC 1272). The weakness left by original sin remains, and the struggle against sin continues; but the baptized are never alone in that struggle.
The seal of the Spirit

Baptism, Chrismation (Confirmation) and the Holy Eucharist together are the sacraments of Christian initiation (CCC 1212). Chrismation completes baptismal grace: the baptized are anointed with Holy Myron (Chrism), consecrated by the bishop, and receive the Holy Spirit as the apostles did at Pentecost, to be strong witnesses of Christ (CCC 1285, 1303).
Like Baptism, Chrismation marks the soul with an indelible character and is received only once (CCC 1304).
Parents and godparents

Children are baptized in the faith of the Church, and parents promise to raise them in that faith (CCC 1250–1253). Godparents (sponsors) must be practicing Catholics who have received the sacraments of initiation, chosen to help the child live as a Christian. They are not chosen only for family honor.
Choosing a Christian name, often the name of a saint, gives the child a heavenly friend and a model (CCC 2156).
In danger of death

In an emergency anyone, even a non-baptized person, can baptize, if he or she intends to do what the Church does: pour water on the head of the person, saying, “N., I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1256). Inform the parish priest afterwards, so that it can be recorded and the other rites completed.

Those who die for the faith before being baptized (baptism of blood), and catechumens who die with the explicit desire for Baptism, are saved without the sacrament (CCC 1258–1259). For children who die without Baptism, the Church entrusts them to the mercy of God and hopes for their salvation (CCC 1261).
Living our Baptism

Remember the date of your Baptism and celebrate it. Renew your baptismal promises at Easter. Teach children that the font is where they were born as Christians. Visit your baptismal church when you can.
The white garment and the lighted candle given at Baptism are a call: keep the garment clean and the light burning until the Lord comes (cf. Matthew 25:1–13).
notes: Parents should ask for the Baptism of their children within the first weeks after birth and prepare for it; delay without a just reason is not right (CCC 1250; CCEO c. 686; c. 867).
Baptism must be recorded in the parish register; the baptismal certificate is needed for later sacraments, especially marriage.
A godparent must be at least sixteen years old (unless the bishop decides otherwise), confirmed, living a life of faith, and not the father or mother of the child (c. 874; CCEO c. 685).
Baptism validly given in other Christian Churches is not repeated when a person enters full communion with the Catholic Church.
Candidates for Confirmation must be in a state of grace; they should go to Confession beforehand (CCC 1310).
Catholics of the Eastern Churches who were chrismated at Baptism are already confirmed; they must not be confirmed again in the Latin Church.

sub: The sacrament of Christ's healing for the seriously ill and the elderly, with Viaticum and the last rites of the Roman Rite
sec: Christ the healer and the apostolic Church

The Gospels are full of the sick who came to Jesus: the blind, the lepers, the paralyzed, the woman who touched the fringe of his cloak. He healed them as a sign that the Kingdom of God had come, and he took our weakness upon himself (Matthew 8:17). When he sent out the Twelve, they “anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them” (Mark 6:13).

The apostolic Church continued this ministry: “Are any among you sick? They should call for the elders of the church and have them pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord. The prayer of faith will save the sick, and the Lord will raise them up; and anyone who has committed sins will be forgiven” (James 5:14–15). As early as the year 416 Pope Innocent I, writing to Bishop Decentius of Gubbio, cited this text and explained that the oil blessed by the bishop is for the anointing of the sick faithful (CCC 1510–1512).
From “Extreme Unction” to “Anointing of the Sick”

Over the centuries the sacrament was more and more delayed until the very end of life, and in the West it came to be called “Extreme Unction”, the last anointing. The Council of Trent (1551) taught that it is a true sacrament instituted by Christ, insinuated in Mark and promulgated by James, and that its effect is the grace of the Holy Spirit which wipes away the remains of sin, comforts the soul and sometimes restores bodily health.

The Second Vatican Council restored the older understanding: “Extreme Unction, which may also and more fittingly be called Anointing of the Sick, is not a sacrament for those only who are at the point of death” (Sacrosanctum Concilium 73). In 1972 Pope Saint Paul VI promulgated the revised rite with the apostolic constitution Sacram Unctionem Infirmorum, which fixed the present form of words and the anointing of the forehead and hands.
Who should receive it, and when

The Anointing is for any of the faithful who, having reached the use of reason, begins to be in danger because of sickness or old age (c. 1004 §1). It is fitting before a serious operation, in a grave or chronic illness, for the elderly who have become notably weak even without a particular disease, and for sick children who have enough use of reason to be strengthened by it (CCC 1514–1515).

It may be repeated when the sick person recovers and falls ill again, or when the illness becomes more serious during the same sickness (c. 1004 §2). Do not wait until the person is unconscious. The sacrament is best received while the sick person can still pray, confess, and receive Holy Communion with the family around the bed.
The oil of the sick and the Chrism Mass

The matter of the sacrament is oil, normally olive oil, or in case of need another oil from plants. The Oil of the Sick (Oleum infirmorum) is blessed by the bishop at the Chrism Mass, celebrated on the morning of Holy Thursday or on another day close to it, together with the Oil of Catechumens and the consecration of the holy Chrism. The priests of the diocese then carry these oils to their parishes.

In true necessity any priest may bless the oil himself, but only within the celebration of the sacrament (c. 999). The parish keeps the holy oils in a dignified place, the ambry; the oil stock a priest carries to the sick is kept clean and refilled, and old oil is burned with reverence when new oil arrives. The oil recalls the Good Samaritan, who poured oil and wine on the wounds of the man left half dead (Luke 10:34).
The rite step by step

The Roman book Pastoral Care of the Sick: Rites of Anointing and Viaticum gives the order. After the greeting, the priest may sprinkle the sick person and the room with holy water, recalling Baptism, and read the words of James 5:14–15. The penitential act follows (or the sacrament of Penance, if the sick person wishes to confess). A short reading from Scripture is proclaimed, and the priest leads a litany of intercession for the sick person and those who care for him or her.

Then come the three central gestures. First, the priest lays his hands on the head of the sick person in silence, as Jesus laid his hands on the sick. Second, he blesses the oil, or, if it is already blessed, prays a prayer of thanksgiving over it, to which all answer, “Blessed be God who heals us in Christ.” Third, he anoints the forehead, saying, “Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit” (R. Amen), and the palms of the hands, saying, “May the Lord who frees you from sin save you and raise you up” (R. Amen). A prayer suited to the person's condition, the Lord's Prayer, Holy Communion if possible, and the blessing conclude the rite (CCC 1513, 1517–1519).
What the sacrament gives

The special grace of the Holy Spirit gives strength, peace and courage to bear the suffering of illness or old age, and protects against the temptation to discouragement and anguish before death. It unites the sick person more closely to the Passion of Christ, so that suffering takes on a new, saving meaning. It forgives sins if the sick person was unable to obtain forgiveness through the sacrament of Penance. It restores health if that is conducive to the salvation of the soul. And it prepares for the passage to eternal life (CCC 1520–1523).

The sick are not useless to the Church. Saint Paul could write, “I am now rejoicing in my sufferings for your sake, and in my flesh I am completing what is lacking in Christ's afflictions for the sake of his body, that is, the church” (Colossians 1:24). Pope Saint John Paul II taught in Salvifici Doloris (1984) that human suffering, joined to Christ, becomes a source of good for the whole Church (CCC 1522).
Viaticum and the last rites

For those who are about to leave this life, the Church offers, besides the Anointing, Holy Communion as Viaticum, the “food for the journey” to the Father. Christ said: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day” (John 6:54; CCC 1524–1525). If possible Viaticum is given within Mass at the bedside; at least, the dying person renews the profession of baptismal faith before receiving it.

When death is near and time is short, the Roman Rite provides a continuous rite: Penance, then the Anointing, then Viaticum, so that, as Baptism, Confirmation and the Eucharist began the Christian life, Penance, Anointing and the Eucharist bring it to completion (CCC 1525). After confession the priest may give the Apostolic Pardon, a plenary indulgence at the hour of death. The book also contains the Commendation of the Dying: short texts of Scripture, litanies and prayers that the family may pray when the priest cannot be present.
How the family and the parish can help

Tell the parish priest early when someone is seriously ill or about to undergo surgery. Prepare the room: a table with a clean white cloth, a crucifix, two lighted candles, holy water, a glass of water and a small spoon if Communion is to be given, and a little cotton wool or bread for the priest's fingers. Switch off the television, gather the family and pray together.

Many parishes in Kerala celebrate the Anointing communally for the elderly and the sick, often on the World Day of the Sick, 11 February, the memorial of Our Lady of Lourdes, or during a parish feast. Visit the sick, pray the rosary with them, bring them Holy Communion through the priest or an extraordinary minister, and support palliative care. “I was sick and you took care of me” (Matthew 25:36).
notes: Only bishops and priests can validly give the Anointing of the Sick; deacons and lay people cannot (CCC 1516; c. 1003 §1; Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, note of 11 February 2005).

When there is doubt whether the sick person has reached the use of reason, is dangerously ill, or is already dead, the sacrament is given (c. 1005). It is not given to those who obstinately persist in manifest grave sin (c. 1007).

The Anointing is not given to the dead. If the priest arrives after death, he prays for the deceased and comforts the family; if it is uncertain whether death has occurred, he may anoint conditionally.
Those who are conscious should go to Confession before the Anointing whenever possible; the Anointing forgives sins only when the sick person cannot confess.
Every Catholic in danger of death from any cause is bound to receive Holy Communion as Viaticum, and pastors must see that it is not delayed (c. 921–922).
In grave necessity a single anointing on the forehead, or on another suitable part of the body, suffices; the full form of words is still said.
refs: Paul VI, Sacram Unctionem Infirmorum (1972); Pastoral Care of the Sick: Rites of Anointing and Viaticum

sub: The sacrament of married love in the Latin Church: God's plan, the Order of Celebrating Matrimony, and Christian family life
sec: God's plan from the beginning

“God created humankind in his image… male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). “Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Marriage is not a human invention or a mere social contract; it is written into creation by God himself, for the good of the spouses and the procreation and education of children (CCC 1601–1605; c. 1055 §1).

Jesus restored marriage to its original dignity: “what God has joined together, let no one separate” (Mark 10:9). For the baptized it is a sacrament. The love of husband and wife becomes a living sign of the love of Christ for his Church, as Saint Paul says: “This is a great mystery, and I am applying it to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32; CCC 1612–1617). The first sign Jesus worked, at the wedding at Cana, shows that he blesses married love (John 2:1–11).
The marks of Christian marriage

Unity: one man and one woman, giving themselves to each other for life. Indissolubility: a valid sacramental marriage, once consummated, cannot be dissolved by any human power, only by death (CCC 1640, 2382; c. 1141). Fidelity: an exclusive love, without betrayal in body or heart. Openness to life: children are the supreme gift of marriage, and parents are the first teachers of the faith to their children (CCC 1652–1653).

Free consent is the heart of marriage. No one may be forced to marry; consent given under grave fear, or obtained by deceit about a quality that seriously disturbs married life, can make a marriage invalid (CCC 1625–1628; cc. 1098, 1103). This is why the Church asks careful questions before the wedding and why parents, however loving, must not decide in place of their children.
Who marries whom: ministers and form

In the Latin tradition the spouses themselves are the ministers of the sacrament: they confer it on each other by expressing their consent before the Church (CCC 1623). The bishop, priest or deacon who assists asks for their consent and receives it in the name of the Church, and gives the Church's blessing. Two witnesses must also be present (c. 1108).

The Roman book is the Order of Celebrating Matrimony (second typical edition, 1991; new English translation in use from 2016). It provides three forms: within Mass, which is normal when both are Catholic; without Mass, within a Liturgy of the Word; and a form for marriage between a Catholic and a catechumen or a non-Christian. In each, the Word of God, the consent and the blessing are the essential moments.
The rite step by step

After the entrance and the Liturgy of the Word (readings may include Genesis 2, Tobit 8, the Song of Songs, 1 Corinthians 13, Ephesians 5 and John 2) and the homily, the priest questions the couple: “have you come here to enter into marriage without coercion, freely and wholeheartedly?”; “Are you prepared, as you follow the path of marriage, to love and honor each other for as long as you both shall live?”; and “Are you prepared to accept children lovingly from God and to bring them up according to the law of Christ and his Church?” Each answers, “I have” and “I am.”

Joining their right hands, they declare their consent: “I, N., take you, N., to be my wife (husband). I promise to be faithful to you, in good times and in bad, in sickness and in health, to love you and to honor you all the days of my life.” The priest receives it with the words: “May the Lord in his kindness strengthen the consent you have declared before the Church… What God joins together, let no one put asunder.” The rings are blessed and exchanged: “N., receive this ring as a sign of my love and fidelity. In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” After the Lord's Prayer the priest, with hands extended over the couple, sings or says the Nuptial Blessing, asking God to send the Holy Spirit upon them, and the couple receive Holy Communion together.
Indian and Kerala customs

The Church welcomes the good customs of each people (Sacrosanctum Concilium 77). In India, where the bishops have approved it, the tying of the thali or minnu by the bridegroom, the giving of the wedding saree (mantrakodi) and the exchange of garlands may follow the blessing and exchange of rings, with a prayer of blessing. These signs say in our own language what the ring says: belonging, fidelity and care.

In Kerala Latin parishes, the formal betrothal (manasammatham) is usually held in the church some weeks before the wedding, in the presence of the families and the parish priest, and the banns of marriage are announced in the parishes of both parties so that any impediment can be made known (c. 1067). The family feast that follows should be joyful, simple and generous to the poor, never a show of wealth.
Preparing well

Marriage is prepared long before the wedding: by chaste friendship, by prayer, and by honest conversation about faith, children, money, work and the two families. Kerala dioceses require couples to attend a marriage preparation course run by the family apostolate and to meet the parish priest in good time with their baptismal certificates and documents of freedom to marry. Pope Francis asks that preparation continue after the wedding, accompanying young couples in their first years (Amoris Laetitia 205–211, 217–230).

The couple should go to Confession before the wedding and receive Holy Communion, so that they begin their married life in grace (CCC 1622). It helps to choose the readings together, to pray for each other daily, and to ask the blessing of their parents, as Tobias and Sarah prayed together on their wedding night (Tobit 8:4–8).
When a Catholic marries someone of another Church or faith

In Kerala marriages between Latin Catholics and Syro-Malabar or Syro-Malankara Catholics are common. Both are Catholics; the wedding normally takes place in the parish of the bride or the bridegroom. Because the Eastern Churches require the blessing of a priest for validity, a deacon cannot validly assist at a marriage when either party belongs to an Eastern Church (c. 1108 §3, as amended in 2016). The children are ascribed to the Church of the father unless both parents agree to ascribe them to the Latin Church (c. 111 §1).

A marriage with a baptized non-Catholic Christian (for example Orthodox, Jacobite, Mar Thoma or CSI) requires the permission of the local Ordinary; with a non-baptized person a dispensation from the impediment of disparity of worship is needed. The Catholic party declares that he or she will avoid dangers of falling away from the faith and sincerely promises to do all in his or her power to have the children baptized and brought up in the Catholic Church; the other party is informed of this promise (CCC 1633–1637; cc. 1124–1129).
Living the sacrament

The grace of the sacrament remains every day: it gives the spouses strength to love, to forgive, to bear one another's burdens and to raise their children in the faith. “Love is patient; love is kind; love is not envious or boastful or arrogant or rude” (1 Corinthians 13:4–5). A family that prays together in the evening, goes to Mass together on Sunday and forgives each other becomes a domestic church (CCC 1655–1658).

When difficulties come, seek help early: from a priest, a trusted Catholic counselor, the diocesan family center, or an older couple in the parish. Christ who was present at Cana is present in every Christian marriage, and his mother still says, “Do whatever he tells you” (John 2:5).
notes: Catholics must marry according to the canonical form, before the local Ordinary, the parish priest or a priest or deacon delegated by them, and two witnesses; otherwise the marriage is invalid unless a dispensation from the form has been given (c. 1108; cc. 1117, 1127).
Marriage with a baptized non-Catholic requires permission; marriage with a non-baptized person requires a dispensation from disparity of worship, without which it is invalid (cc. 1086, 1124–1125).

Civil divorce does not dissolve a valid sacramental marriage. Where there is serious doubt about validity, the diocesan tribunal can examine the case and, if nullity is proved, declare that a true marriage never existed (CCC 1629). Pope Francis simplified this process in Mitis Iudex Dominus Iesus (2015).
When either party is an Eastern Catholic or an Eastern non-Catholic, only a priest, not a deacon, can validly assist at the marriage (c. 1108 §3; Pope Francis, De concordia inter Codices, 2016).

Dowry is forbidden by Indian law (Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961) and contradicts the dignity of the sacrament; the bishops of Kerala have repeatedly asked the faithful to reject it and to avoid extravagant weddings.
Engaged couples should not live together before marriage; the Church asks them to keep chastity in preparation for the gift of themselves (CCC 2350).
refs: Genesis 1:27–28; 2:24; Tobit 8:4–8; Mark 10:6–9; John 2:1–11; 1 Corinthians 13; Ephesians 5:21–33

sub: Bishops, priests and deacons in the Latin Church: the call, the formation, and the rites of ordination
sec: The priesthood of Christ

Christ is the one High Priest, “holy, blameless, undefiled”, who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:26–27). All the baptized share in his priesthood: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's own people” (1 Peter 2:9), offering their lives as a spiritual sacrifice (CCC 1546). This common priesthood of the faithful is the foundation of all Christian life.

But Christ also chose the Twelve and gave them a special share in his mission: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19); “As the Father has sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21). Through the sacrament of Holy Orders this mission continues in the Church until the end of time. The ministerial priesthood differs from the common priesthood in essence and not only in degree: those ordained act in the person of Christ the Head, to teach, to sanctify and to shepherd his people (Lumen Gentium 10; CCC 1547–1553).
Three degrees of one sacrament

The bishop receives the fullness of the sacrament. He is a successor of the apostles, a member of the college of bishops with and under the Pope, and the visible principle of unity in his local Church, where he teaches, sanctifies and governs (CCC 1555–1561). The priest is the co-worker of the bishop: he celebrates the Eucharist, forgives sins, anoints the sick, preaches the Word and cares for the people entrusted to him, usually as parish priest or assistant (CCC 1562–1568).

The deacon is ordained “not for priesthood but for service” (Lumen Gentium 29). He proclaims the Gospel and may preach, assists at the altar, baptizes, assists at marriages where permitted, brings Viaticum, leads funerals and serves the poor (CCC 1569–1571). In the Latin Church every priest is first ordained deacon (the transitional diaconate); since the Second Vatican Council the permanent diaconate, open also to married men of mature age, has been restored where the bishops judge it useful.
The essential rite and its effect

The essential sign of Holy Orders in all three degrees is the laying on of hands by the bishop, followed by the consecratory prayer, which asks God to pour out the Holy Spirit and his gifts for the ministry. Pope Pius XII confirmed this in 1947 in the apostolic constitution Sacramentum Ordinis (CCC 1573). Saint Paul reminded Timothy to “rekindle the gift of God that is within you through the laying on of my hands” (2 Timothy 1:6).

Like Baptism and Confirmation, Holy Orders marks the soul with an indelible spiritual character; it cannot be repeated or conferred for a limited time (CCC 1581–1583). Only a baptized man validly receives sacred ordination; the Church holds herself bound by the choice made by the Lord himself (CCC 1577). No one has a right to ordination: it is a call from God, discerned and confirmed by the Church (CCC 1578).
The road to the altar

A Latin candidate normally enters a minor or propaedeutic seminary, then studies philosophy and theology for some seven years or more, with a year of pastoral work, under the Church's norms for priestly formation (The Gift of the Priestly Vocation, 2016). Along the way he is formally admitted to candidacy and is instituted in the ministries of lector and acolyte, which since 1972 have replaced the old minor orders (Paul VI, Ministeria Quaedam). Since 2021 these lay ministries may be conferred on women as well as men (Francis, Spiritus Domini).

Before diaconate the candidate makes a written declaration of freedom, and, in the Latin Church, publicly undertakes the obligation of celibacy (c. 1037), and makes a profession of faith and an oath of fidelity. Kerala's Latin dioceses form their students in their own minor seminaries and in major seminaries such as St Joseph's Pontifical Seminary, Carmelgiri, Aluva, and religious houses of formation; many Kerala priests serve as missionaries in northern India and abroad.
Ordination of a priest, step by step

Ordination takes place within Mass, on a Sunday or feast if possible, with as many of the faithful as can come. After the Gospel the candidate is called by name and answers “Present.” A priest testifies that he has been found worthy, and the bishop chooses him for the Order of the Priesthood; the people respond with approval. After the homily the candidate promises to discharge the office faithfully, to preach, to celebrate the sacraments, to pray, and to be united ever more closely to Christ; then, kneeling and placing his joined hands in the bishop's, he promises respect and obedience to the bishop and his successors.

He lies prostrate while the Litany of the Saints is sung. The bishop lays his hands on his head in silence, and all the priests present do the same, as a sign of their one presbyterate. The bishop sings the Prayer of Ordination. The new priest is vested with the stole worn across both shoulders and with the chasuble; the bishop anoints his palms with holy Chrism, and hands him the paten with the bread and the chalice with the wine, saying: “Receive the oblation of the holy people, to be offered to God. Understand what you do, imitate what you celebrate, and conform your life to the mystery of the Lord's Cross.” The kiss of peace follows, and he concelebrates the Eucharist for the first time.
Ordination of a deacon and of a bishop

At the ordination of a deacon only the bishop lays on hands, for the deacon is ordained for the ministry of the bishop. The new deacon is vested with the stole worn over the left shoulder and with the dalmatic, and receives the Book of the Gospels with the words: “Receive the Gospel of Christ, whose herald you have become. Believe what you read, teach what you believe, and practice what you teach.”

A bishop is ordained by at least three bishops, after the apostolic mandate of the Pope is read. All the bishops lay hands on him, and the open Book of the Gospels is held over his head while the principal consecrator sings the Prayer of Ordination. His head is anointed with Chrism; he receives the Book of the Gospels, the ring as a sign of fidelity to the Church, his bride, the mitre and the pastoral staff, and, if he is the diocesan bishop, is seated on the cathedra (CCC 1559).
Celibacy and the life of the priest

In the Latin Church priests and bishops are chosen from among men who freely embrace celibacy “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:12; c. 277). Celibacy is a gift that frees the priest to give himself entirely to Christ and to the people, and is a sign of the life to come (Presbyterorum Ordinis 16; CCC 1579). The Eastern Churches, including some in communion with Rome, have a long and honored tradition of married priests; in all of them bishops are chosen from among the celibate (CCC 1580).

A diocesan priest belongs to the presbyterate of his diocese and promises obedience to its bishop; a religious priest (for example a Carmelite, Franciscan, Capuchin or Jesuit) lives also by the vows of his order. Every priest is bound to pray the Liturgy of the Hours daily, to live simply, to make a yearly retreat and to keep studying, so that he may serve well.
Praying for vocations and for our priests

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38). The Fourth Sunday of Easter, Good Shepherd Sunday, is the World Day of Prayer for Vocations. Every family can pray for vocations and encourage a son who feels the call, and a daughter who feels called to religious life.

Pray for your priests and bishops every day. Respect them, help them, and correct with charity when needed. A priest is “chosen from among mortals” and “put in charge of things pertaining to God on their behalf” (Hebrews 5:1); he needs the prayer, friendship and honesty of his community.
notes: Only a bishop can validly ordain (CCC 1576; c. 1012). In the Latin Church a bishop may be ordained only with a pontifical mandate; ordaining without it incurs excommunication reserved to the Holy See (c. 1013; c. 1387).
Candidates must be freely chosen, mature, of sound faith and morals, and judged suitable after careful examination; anyone who knows of an impediment is bound to make it known (cc. 1025–1052).

Minimum ages: twenty-five for the priesthood, twenty-three for the transitional diaconate, twenty-five for an unmarried permanent deacon and thirty-five for a married one, with his wife's consent (c. 1031).
Celibacy for priests is a law of the Latin Church, not a doctrine of faith; the Eastern Churches have their own discipline (c. 277; CCEO c. 373). Both are honored in the one Catholic Church.

A priest who leaves the ministry remains a priest by the character received; he may be dispensed from the obligations of the clerical state only by the Holy See. In danger of death any priest may validly absolve (c. 976).
The so-called minor orders and the subdiaconate were suppressed in the Latin Church in 1972; lector and acolyte are now ministries conferred by institution, not orders (Ministeria Quaedam).

sub: Lauds, Vespers and the hours of the Roman Rite: how the Church sanctifies the day with the psalms
sec: Praying without ceasing

“Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). From the beginning God's people prayed at fixed hours. The psalmist says, “Seven times a day I praise you for your righteous ordinances” (Psalm 119:164); Daniel knelt three times a day toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10). After Pentecost the apostles kept the hours of prayer: Peter went up on the roof to pray at about noon, and Peter and John went to the temple at the hour of prayer, at three o'clock in the afternoon (Acts 10:9; 3:1).

The Liturgy of the Hours sanctifies the whole course of the day and night. It extends to every hour the praise and thanksgiving of the Eucharist, which is its center (CCC 1174–1178). It is not a private devotion but the public prayer of the Church: “the very prayer which Christ himself, together with his body, addresses to the Father” (Sacrosanctum Concilium 84).
A short history of the Roman Office

The early Christians gathered especially in the morning and evening for psalms and prayer, and soon also at the third, sixth and ninth hours and at night. The monks of East and West made the Divine Office the center of their life; Saint Benedict told his monks to prefer nothing to the Work of God (Rule, ch. 43). In the Middle Ages the many books were gathered into one portable volume, the breviary, so that clergy could pray it while traveling.

Pope Saint Pius V issued the Roman Breviary in 1568 after the Council of Trent; Pope Saint Pius X reformed its psalter in 1911. The Second Vatican Council asked for a renewal that would restore the true hour of each office and open it to the whole people (Sacrosanctum Concilium 83–101). Pope Saint Paul VI promulgated the new Liturgia Horarum with the apostolic constitution Laudis Canticum (1970); the books appeared in 1971, with a second typical edition in 1985.
The parts of the Liturgy of the Hours

The day opens with the Invitatory, usually Psalm 95, before the first hour prayed. The Office of Readings, which may be prayed at any time of day, contains psalms, a long reading from Scripture and a second reading from the Fathers, the saints or Church documents. Morning Prayer (Lauds) and Evening Prayer (Vespers) are the two hinges of the day and the principal hours (Sacrosanctum Concilium 89).

Daytime Prayer may be said at mid-morning, midday or mid-afternoon (Terce, Sext, None). Night Prayer (Compline) is the last prayer before sleep. The psalms are distributed over a four-week cycle (the Psalter); the Proper of Seasons follows Advent, Christmas, Lent and Easter; the Proper of Saints and the Commons provide for feasts and memorials. The General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours (1971) explains everything in detail.
Morning Prayer, step by step

If it is the first hour of the day, it begins with the Invitatory: “Lord, open my lips. And my mouth will proclaim your praise” (cf. Psalm 51:15), with Psalm 95 and its antiphon. Otherwise it begins: “God, come to my assistance. Lord, make haste to help me. Glory to the Father…” (cf. Psalm 70:1). A hymn follows, then the psalmody: a morning psalm, a canticle from the Old Testament, and a psalm of praise, each with its antiphon and ending with the Glory be.

Then come a short reading from Scripture and a short responsory, and the Gospel canticle, the Benedictus, the song of Zechariah: “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has looked favorably on his people and redeemed them” (Luke 1:68–79), during which all make the sign of the cross. Intercessions consecrate the day and its work to God, followed by the Lord's Prayer, the concluding prayer and, when a priest or deacon presides, the blessing and dismissal.
Evening and Night Prayer

Evening Prayer has the same shape: introduction, hymn, two psalms and a New Testament canticle, short reading and responsory, the Magnificat of Mary, “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior” (Luke 1:46–47), intercessions (the last always for the dead), the Lord's Prayer and the concluding prayer. It recalls the evening sacrifice of the temple: “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 141:2). On solemnities incense may be used at the Magnificat.

Night Prayer begins with an examination of conscience and an act of sorrow, then one or two psalms (such as Psalms 4, 91 or 134), a short reading, the responsory “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit”, and the Nunc Dimittis, the song of Simeon: “Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word” (Luke 2:29–32). After the prayer comes the blessing, “May the all-powerful Lord grant us a restful night and a peaceful death”, and an antiphon to Our Lady: the Salve Regina, or in their seasons the Alma Redemptoris Mater, Ave Regina Caelorum and Regina Caeli.
Praying the psalms with Christ

The psalms are the prayer book of Israel and of Jesus himself. He prayed them in the synagogue and on the Cross (Matthew 27:46; Luke 23:46). When we pray them, Christ prays in us and for us, and we pray to him. The psalms hold every human feeling: praise, thanksgiving, trust, sorrow, anger, longing; by praying them in the name of the whole Church we learn to carry the joys and sufferings of all people before God (General Instruction 100–109).

Saint Augustine taught, in sense: if the psalm prays, pray; if it laments, lament; if it rejoices, rejoice; if it hopes, hope. Antiphons, psalm titles and psalm prayers help us read each psalm in the light of Christ. Some harsh verses are omitted in the liturgy; those that remain teach us to hand our anger and the injustice of the world to God instead of taking revenge.
The Hours in Kerala Latin parishes

Priests, deacons and religious in Kerala pray the Hours daily, in Latin, English or Malayalam; Malayalam books of the Hours for the Latin Church have been prepared through the Kerala Latin liturgical commission and are used in religious houses and seminaries. Many religious communities pray Morning and Evening Prayer in common, and some parishes sing Vespers on Sundays and feasts.

Among the laity, the Angelus at six in the morning, at noon and at six in the evening, announced by the church bell, and the family evening prayer at the lighting of the lamp with the Rosary, keep alive the ancient instinct to sanctify the hours. These devotions are a natural bridge to the Liturgy of the Hours itself, which the Church warmly recommends to lay people (Sacrosanctum Concilium 100).
How to begin

Begin small: pray Morning Prayer or Evening Prayer once a day with an approved book or app, or Night Prayer before sleep, which is short and the same every week. Learn the Benedictus, the Magnificat and the Nunc Dimittis by heart; they are Gospel prayers that every Christian can carry through life.

Pray the hours as close as possible to their true time, unhurried, with pauses of silence (General Instruction 202). When you pray even one psalm with the Church, your small prayer joins the great prayer of priests, religious and faithful all over the world, and the praise of heaven.
notes: Priests and transitional deacons are bound to pray the full Liturgy of the Hours daily; permanent deacons pray the part determined by the conference of bishops (c. 276 §2, 3°). Religious pray according to their constitutions (c. 663 §3).

Morning and Evening Prayer are the principal hours and should not be omitted without a serious reason (General Instruction 29). The Office of Readings may be anticipated on the previous evening, after Evening Prayer.

Communal celebration is preferred to private recitation, but the Liturgy of the Hours prayed alone by a priest, religious or lay person is still the prayer of the Church (Sacrosanctum Concilium 99–100; General Instruction 9, 33).
Only approved texts may be used in the liturgy; check that apps and booklets follow the books approved for your country and language.
The Office of the Dead and the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary are older devotional forms; the Liturgy of the Hours itself contains offices for the dead and memorials of Our Lady.
Translations: a revised English translation of the Liturgy of the Hours has been introduced in several English-speaking countries since 2024; follow what your diocese has authorized.

sub: Holy water, the crucifix, the rosary, blessings, Benediction and the popular piety of Latin Catholics
sec: What sacramentals are

Sacramentals are sacred signs instituted by the Church which resemble the sacraments: they signify effects, especially spiritual ones, obtained through the prayer of the Church. By them people are disposed to receive the chief effect of the sacraments, and various occasions in life are made holy (Sacrosanctum Concilium 60; CCC 1667–1670).

The difference is important. The seven sacraments were instituted by Christ and give grace by the very rite performed. Sacramentals were instituted by the Church; they do not give the grace of the Holy Spirit in the way the sacraments do, but through the Church's prayer they prepare us to receive grace and to cooperate with it. Among them are blessings, the consecration of churches and altars, the profession of religious, and blessed objects such as holy water, candles, ashes, palms, crucifixes, medals, the rosary and the scapular.
Blessings come first

Every blessing is first praise of God for his gifts, and then a prayer for his help. God blessed his people through the priests of Israel: “The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you, and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you, and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24–26). Jesus blessed the children, laying his hands on them (Mark 10:16), and blessed the bread before he broke it. “For everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected, provided it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by God's word and by prayer” (1 Timothy 4:4–5).

The Roman Book of Blessings (De Benedictionibus, 1984) gives each blessing a simple shape: a greeting and introduction; a reading from the Word of God; intercessions; the prayer of blessing; and often an outward sign, such as the sign of the cross, the laying on of hands, sprinkling with holy water or incense; then the conclusion. The Word of God comes first, so that a blessing is never a magic formula but a moment of faith (CCC 1671–1672).
Who may bless

Bishops, priests and deacons preside at most blessings, according to their ministry. Some blessings, especially those that consecrate persons or places permanently, such as the dedication of a church, an altar or a chalice, are reserved to the bishop or priest (c. 1169). But because every baptized person shares in the priesthood of Christ, lay people may give certain blessings, with the forms and words provided for them (CCC 1669; c. 1168).

Parents especially may bless their children: tracing the sign of the cross on a child's forehead at night, before an examination or a journey, is a true Christian blessing. Catechists and leaders of family units may lead blessings of the home and of meals. In these lay blessings the leader says “May God bless us” rather than “I bless you”, and does not use gestures proper to the ordained.
Not magic, but faith

A sacramental does not work by itself like a charm. Its power comes from the prayer of the Church and from the faith and love with which it is used (CCC 1670). Holy water on the forehead recalls our Baptism; a blessed cross in the home declares that Christ is its Lord; the rosary leads us to meditate on the mysteries of Christ with Mary. If faith is absent, the object profits nothing.

Superstition gives to signs a power they do not have; it is a sin against the first commandment (CCC 2111). Fortune-telling, horoscopes, consulting astrologers before weddings or house-building, charms against the evil eye, and chain messages that threaten misfortune if not forwarded are contrary to faith and must be avoided (CCC 2116–2117). Be careful too with “healing oils”, private revelations and prayers not approved by the Church.
Holy water and the sacramentals of the Roman year

Holy water is the most familiar sacramental: the faithful sign themselves with it as they enter the church, remembering Baptism. On Sundays, especially in Easter Time, the rite of blessing and sprinkling of water may replace the penitential act at Mass. Water blessed at the Easter Vigil is taken home by many families.

The Roman year is rich in blessed signs. On 2 February, the Presentation of the Lord, candles are blessed and carried in procession for Christ, the light of the nations. On 3 February, the memorial of Saint Blaise, throats are blessed with two crossed candles: “Through the intercession of Saint Blaise, bishop and martyr, may God deliver you from every disease of the throat and from every other illness.” On Ash Wednesday ashes are placed on the head: “Repent, and believe in the Gospel” or “Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return.” Palms are blessed on Palm Sunday and kept in homes until they are burned for the next year's ashes.
Devotions of the Latin tradition

The Rosary, with its Joyful, Luminous, Sorrowful and Glorious mysteries (the Luminous mysteries were added by Saint John Paul II in 2002), the Angelus, the Way of the Cross on the Fridays of Lent, the brown scapular of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, the Miraculous Medal, the Chaplet of Divine Mercy and the devotion to the Sacred Heart of Jesus on First Fridays are among the most loved devotions of Latin Catholics. Each one leads to the mysteries of Christ.

Eucharistic adoration has a special place. In Benediction of the Blessed Sacrament the Host is exposed in the monstrance; after hymns, readings, silent adoration and the Tantum Ergo, the priest or deacon blesses the people with the Sacrament, and the Divine Praises are said. The rite is found in the book Holy Communion and Worship of the Eucharist outside Mass (1973). Here it is Christ himself who blesses.
Popular piety on the Kerala coast

The faith of the Latin Catholics of Kerala is expressed in feasts and processions with flags, statues and music; novenas, such as the Tuesday novena of Saint Antony and the novena of Our Lady of Perpetual Help; pilgrimages to shrines such as the Basilica of Our Lady of Ransom at Vallarpadam, Saint Andrew's Basilica at Arthunkal with its feast of Saint Sebastian, the Madre de Deus church at Vettucaud, and Saint Xavier's at Kottar. In fishing villages, boats and nets are blessed before the season, and the Book of Blessings has an order for blessing boats and fishing gear.

The Church values this popular piety, purifies it and guides it, so that it leads to Christ and to the liturgy and is not separated from charity and justice (CCC 1674–1676; Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy, 2001). Vows and offerings (nercha) at shrines are good when they come from faith and gratitude, never when they become a bargain with God or a substitute for conversion. A feast is well kept when the poor of the parish are also fed.
Blessings in daily life

Ask the priest to bless your home, especially when you move in and in Easter Time; to bless a new vehicle, a shop, a boat or a place of work. Keep holy water at home and use it with a prayer. Enthrone a picture of the Sacred Heart or of Our Lady in the family's prayer corner.

Before meals pray, “Bless us, O Lord, and these your gifts, which we are about to receive from your bounty, through Christ our Lord. Amen”, and give thanks afterwards. At the start of a journey, in times of sickness or fear, a short blessing turns ordinary life into prayer and reminds us that the whole world belongs to God.
notes: Blessed objects should be treated with reverence and not used for profane purposes; when worn out, they are burned or buried, not thrown away with rubbish (c. 1171).

Exorcism in the strict sense may be performed only by a priest with the express permission of the local bishop (CCC 1673; c. 1172). Those who believe they are troubled should first see a priest and, where needed, a doctor; many troubles have natural or psychological causes.
Do not buy or sell anything for its blessing; the price paid is only for the material of the object. Trading in sacred things is simony.

Indulgences are a remission before God of temporal punishment for sins already forgiven, granted through the Church under conditions (sacramental Confession, Holy Communion, prayer for the Pope's intentions, detachment from sin). The current norms are in the Enchiridion of Indulgences (CCC 1471–1479; c. 992).
Sacramentals are for everyone: catechumens, and even non-Catholics, may receive blessings unless the Church has forbidden it in a particular case (c. 1170).
No devotion, however dear, replaces Sunday Mass and the sacraments; devotions are meant to lead to them (Sacrosanctum Concilium 13).
refs: Book of Blessings (De Benedictionibus, 1984); Holy Communion and Worship of the Eucharist outside Mass (1973)
Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy (2001); John Paul II, Rosarium Virginis Mariae (2002)

sub: How the Latin Church accompanies the dead and comforts the living: the vigil, the funeral Mass, the committal and the prayer that continues
sec: Christian hope before death

“I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live, and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 11:25–26). For Christians death is not the end but a passage. The preface of the Mass for the dead says that for your faithful, Lord, life is changed, not ended, and when this earthly dwelling turns to dust, an eternal dwelling is made ready in heaven (CCC 1012). The body that was the temple of the Holy Spirit will rise again on the last day.

Therefore the Church accompanies her children to the end. The Christian funeral is not a sacrament, but a liturgical celebration in which the Church expresses her communion with the dead, asks for them the help of God's mercy, honors their bodies with reverence, and proclaims eternal life to the community gathered (CCC 1680–1684).
Praying for the dead

Scripture praises prayer for the dead: Judas Maccabeus made atonement for those who had died, that they might be delivered from their sin, and the sacred writer calls this a holy and pious thought (2 Maccabees 12:43–46). Those who die in God's grace and friendship but are not yet fully purified are assured of eternal salvation, but undergo purification after death, which the Church calls purgatory (CCC 1030–1032).

Our prayers, above all the Eucharistic sacrifice offered for them, and our almsgiving and works of penance, help the departed. The Latin tradition knows the Gregorian Masses, thirty Masses offered on consecutive days for one deceased person, and the plenary indulgence, applicable only to the souls in purgatory, for visiting a cemetery and praying for the dead from 1 to 8 November. The communion of saints unites the living and the dead in one family of God.
The Order of Christian Funerals

The Roman book is the Order of Christian Funerals (Ordo Exsequiarum, 1969). It follows the body of the deceased in three stations, like a journey: the vigil for the deceased, at home or in the church; the funeral liturgy, normally the funeral Mass; and the rite of committal at the grave. Shorter prayers are provided for the moment after death, for gathering in the presence of the body, and for the transfer of the body to the church.

The Church asks that the funeral be marked by hope, simplicity and prayer. The liturgy does not hide the reality of death, but it places it within the Paschal Mystery: the deceased was baptized into Christ's death, and so hopes to share his Resurrection (Romans 6:3–5).
Prayers after death and the vigil

When death comes, the family may gather around the body and pray: a psalm, a short reading, the Lord's Prayer, and the ancient prayer, “Eternal rest grant unto him (her), O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon him (her). May he (she) rest in peace. Amen.” The body is washed and dressed with reverence, a crucifix and lighted candles are placed nearby, and holy water is kept at hand for the visitors to sprinkle.

The vigil is a celebration of the Word of God led by a priest, deacon or lay minister: greeting, an opening song, a prayer, readings from Scripture, a short homily, intercessions, the Lord's Prayer, a concluding prayer and a blessing. In Kerala the wake at home usually continues through the night with the Rosary, Bible readings and hymns; this is a beautiful work of mercy, and the noise and expense of worldly display should give way to prayer.
The funeral Mass, step by step

The priest meets the body at the door of the church. He sprinkles the coffin with holy water, recalling Baptism, and a white pall may be placed over it, recalling the baptismal garment. The coffin is carried in and placed near the Easter candle, the sign of the risen Christ; a Gospel book, a Bible or a cross may be placed on it. Vestments are violet, black or, where the bishops allow, white. The readings may include “the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God, and no torment will ever touch them” (Wisdom 3:1), Romans 6, 1 Thessalonians 4 or John 11 and 14. The homily speaks of God's mercy and the Paschal Mystery; it is not a eulogy.

After the Prayer after Communion comes the final commendation and farewell. The priest invites all to pray in silence; he sprinkles the coffin with holy water and incenses it; the song of farewell is sung; and he says the prayer of commendation, entrusting the deceased to the Father. As the body is carried out the antiphon is sung: “May the angels lead you into paradise; may the martyrs come to welcome you and take you to the holy city, the new and eternal Jerusalem.”
The committal at the grave

At the cemetery the grave, if not already blessed, is blessed. The priest says the prayer of committal, giving the body to the earth in the sure and certain hope of the resurrection. Intercessions, the Lord's Prayer and a concluding prayer follow, and the people may sing a song and throw a little earth into the grave as a last gesture of love.

“For if we live, we live to the Lord, and if we die, we die to the Lord; so then, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's” (Romans 14:8). Catholic cemeteries are blessed places, signs of the faith that the dead are sleeping in Christ, awaiting the resurrection; they should be kept clean, peaceful and well cared for.
After the funeral: remembering the dead

Latin Catholic families in Kerala commonly have Mass offered for the deceased on the seventh day, on the thirtieth or forty-first day, and every year on the anniversary, and invite the family and neighbors to pray. On All Souls' Day (2 November) the parish celebrates Mass for all the dead, and families visit and clean the graves, light candles and pray; on that day every priest may celebrate three Masses.

These customs are good when they express faith and charity. The anniversary meal should be simple; it is better to give alms to the poor and to have Masses offered than to spend on display. Remember the dead by name in the family evening prayer, and teach children to pray, “Eternal rest grant unto them, O Lord.”
Grief and consolation

“Jesus began to weep” at the tomb of his friend Lazarus (John 11:35). Christian faith does not forbid tears; it gives them hope. Paul writes so that we “may not grieve as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). Families should be allowed to grieve, and the parish should surround them with prayer, presence and practical help.

Visit the bereaved after the funeral, not only on the day; widows, widowers and children need care for months and years. Teach children that we will see our loved ones again in Christ, when “he will wipe every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; mourning and crying and pain will be no more” (Revelation 21:4).
notes: The Church earnestly recommends burial of the body. Cremation is permitted when it is not chosen for reasons contrary to Christian faith; the ashes must be kept in a sacred place (cemetery or church), not scattered, divided, made into jewelry or kept at home (CDF, Ad resurgendum cum Christo, 2016; c. 1176 §3).

Church funeral rites are to be denied, unless some sign of repentance was shown before death, to notorious apostates, heretics and schismatics, to those who chose cremation for reasons opposed to the faith, and to other manifest sinners whose funeral would cause public scandal; in doubt the bishop decides (c. 1184).

Pastors should show special compassion to families after tragic deaths, including suicide. The Church does not despair of the salvation of anyone who has taken his or her own life, and prays for them (CCC 2282–2283).

The local Ordinary may permit Church funeral rites for catechumens, for children whose parents intended to have them baptized but who died before Baptism, and in some cases for baptized non-Catholics (c. 1183).

The funeral Mass is not celebrated on the Sundays of Advent, Lent and Easter, on solemnities of obligation, on Holy Thursday or during the Easter Triduum; the funeral is then held with a Liturgy of the Word, and a Mass offered later (GIRM 380).
In the funeral rites there must be no favoritism of persons, and the poor must not be deprived of a fitting funeral (c. 1181).
refs: Wisdom 3:1–9; 2 Maccabees 12:38–46; John 11:17–44; Romans 6:3–9; 14:7–9; 1 Corinthians 15; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18; Revelation 21:1–5
