t: The Story of the Latin Church in India
sub: From the first Latin bishop at Quilon to the Latin dioceses of Kerala today: missions, Padroado and Propaganda, saints, and the coast
sec: Before the Portuguese: the first Latin bishop at Quilon

When the first Latin missionaries reached India, they found a Church already here: the ancient St Thomas Christians of Malabar, with their own bishops from the East Syrian Church and their own liturgy. The Latin Church in India must always remember this with gratitude and respect. The first Latin visitors were travelers and friars: the Franciscan John of Montecorvino stayed at Mylapore on his way to China around 1291, and the Dominican Jordanus Catalani of Séverac worked on the western coast in the 1320s and wrote a description of India's wonders.

In 1329 Pope John XXII erected the diocese of Quilon (Columbum) and named Jordanus its first bishop. This was the first Latin diocese in India. Around 1348 the papal legate John de Marignolli stayed at Quilon and found a Latin church dedicated to Saint George. After this the small Latin community seems to have faded, and little is known of it for nearly two centuries; the records are scarce, and we should not claim more than they show.
The Portuguese and the Padroado

Vasco da Gama reached the Malabar coast near Calicut in 1498, and in 1500 Pedro Álvares Cabral's fleet brought Franciscan friars to Cochin. Through a series of papal bulls in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries the Popes granted the Portuguese crown the Padroado (patronage): the right and the duty to send and support missionaries, build churches and present bishops in the lands it reached. Goa became a diocese in 1534 and an archdiocese in 1558; in the same year Pope Paul IV erected the diocese of Cochin, with its cathedral of Santa Cruz.

The Padroado brought much good: churches, schools, hospitals, printing presses and generations of devoted missionaries. It also tied the Gospel closely to a colonial power. Some methods of that age, including pressure on non-Christians and the Inquisition set up at Goa in 1560, are remembered with sorrow; in the Jubilee of 2000 Pope Saint John Paul II asked forgiveness for the sins of Christians committed in the service of truth. A balanced history gives thanks for the faith that was planted and honestly acknowledges the wounds.
Saint Francis Xavier, apostle of the coast

Francis Xavier, one of the first companions of Saint Ignatius of Loyola, landed at Goa on 6 May 1542 as papal nuncio and missionary. He worked first among the Parava fishermen of the Fishery Coast in the south of today's Tamil Nadu, and in 1544 on the Travancore coast among the Mukkuva fishing people, where he wrote that he baptized some ten thousand people in a single month. He went from village to village ringing a small bell, gathering children and adults to learn the Creed, the Our Father, the Hail Mary and the Commandments in their own language, and he left catechists in each place.

Many coastal churches from Kanyakumari northwards trace their origin to his visits; the church at Kottar, now the cathedral of the Kottar diocese, is one of the most famous. He left India for Malacca, the Moluccas and Japan, and died on the island of Sancian off China on 3 December 1552. His incorrupt body rests in the Basilica of Bom Jesus at Goa. He was canonized in 1622 and in 1927 was named patron of the missions with Saint Thérèse of Lisieux. His motto was the Lord's question: “For what will it profit them to gain the whole world and forfeit their life?” (Mark 8:36).
Goa, Joseph Vaz and the wider Latin Church in India

Goa became the center of the Latin Church in Asia, with its cathedral, seminaries and colleges, and a deeply rooted Konkani Catholic culture. From it missionaries went out across India and beyond. The Jesuit Roberto de Nobili lived as a Brahmin sannyasi at Madurai from 1606 to make the Gospel understood in Tamil culture; Saint John de Britto was martyred at Oriyur in 1693. Latin missions later grew in Mangalore, Bombay, Madras, Bengal, the north-east and the tribal regions of central India.

Saint Joseph Vaz (1651–1711), a priest born at Benaulim in Goa and a member of the Oratory of Goa, worked first in Kanara and then went secretly to Ceylon in 1687, where the Catholics were without priests under Dutch rule. Disguised as a laborer, he revived the Church there, cared for victims of smallpox and wrote prayers and catechisms in Sinhala and Tamil. He died at Kandy on 16 January 1711, was beatified in 1995 and canonized by Pope Francis in Colombo on 14 January 2015. He is a sign that India's Latin Catholics are themselves missionaries.
The St Thomas Christians and the Latin missionaries

The meeting between the Portuguese and the St Thomas Christians began in friendship but became painful. Under the Padroado, Latin bishops were placed over the St Thomas Christians, and the Synod of Diamper (Udayamperoor) in 1599, presided over by Archbishop Aleixo de Menezes of Goa, imposed many Latin customs on their liturgy and law. Resentment grew, and in 1653 a large part of the community took the Coonan Cross Oath at Mattancherry, refusing obedience to the Jesuit archbishop. From the divisions that followed came, over time, the different Churches of the Malankara tradition.

The Catholic Church today speaks of this history with humility. The Eastern Churches have equal dignity with the Latin Church and the right to govern themselves according to their own traditions (Orientalium Ecclesiarum 3, 5). The Syro-Malabar Church received its own hierarchy in 1923 and became a major archiepiscopal Church in 1992; the Syro-Malankara Catholic Church was born from the reunion led by Mar Ivanios in 1930. Latin Catholics in Kerala honor the St Thomas Christians as the elder Church of the land, and live in friendship with the Orthodox, Jacobite and Mar Thoma Churches and with all Christians.
Propaganda Fide and Verapoly

In 1622 Pope Gregory XV founded the Sacred Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith (Propaganda Fide) to direct missions directly from Rome, independently of the colonial crowns. After the Coonan Cross Oath, Propaganda sent Discalced Carmelites from Italy to bring peace among the St Thomas Christians; Bishop Joseph Sebastiani arrived in 1657 and was named Vicar Apostolic of Malabar. When the Dutch captured Cochin in 1663 and expelled the Portuguese clergy, Sebastiani consecrated Parambil Chandy (Alexander de Campo) as bishop for the St Thomas Christians before he left.

From 1673 the Carmelites were allowed to settle at Verapoly (Varapuzha), an island north of Cochin, and it became the seat of the vicariate apostolic for Latin Catholics and, for a long time, for many St Thomas Christians too. The Carmelites opened seminaries and schools and were also scholars: Paulinus of Saint Bartholomew wrote the first printed Sanskrit grammar in Europe (1790), and Clement Peanius's Samkshepavedartham (Rome, 1772) was the first book printed in Malayalam script. For nearly two centuries the Padroado clergy (dependent on Portugal) and the Propaganda clergy (dependent on Rome) worked side by side, sometimes in painful rivalry, a “double jurisdiction” that troubled many parishes until the 1886 settlement.
Quilon, Cochin and the Latin Catholics of the coast

Quilon, the first Latin diocese, was revived as a vicariate apostolic separated from Verapoly in 1845 and became a diocese in 1886. Its Swiss Carmelite bishop Aloysius Maria Benziger (1905–1931) built schools and hospitals and formed a local clergy; Bishop Jerome Fernandez became the first Indian bishop of Quilon in 1937. Cochin, the old Padroado see, continued along the coast to the south and north of the city, and gave birth later to the diocese of Alleppey.

The Latin Catholics of Kerala are found along the whole coast from Kasaragod to Thiruvananthapuram and in the hinterland: fishing communities whose faith goes back to the sixteenth century, families of Portuguese and Anglo-Indian descent, Dalit Christians and others who came to the faith in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Their life has often been hard: poverty, the dangers of the sea, coastal erosion and social discrimination. The Church responded with schools, hospitals, cooperatives and the first religious congregation for women in Kerala, the Teresian Carmelites founded at Koonammavu in 1866 by Mother Eliswa Vakayil with the Carmelite missionary Leopold Beccaro.
Saint Devasahayam, martyr of Travancore

Neelakanta Pillai was born on 23 April 1712 at Nattalam, in today's Kanyakumari district, then part of the kingdom of Travancore. He served in the palace administration of Maharaja Marthanda Varma (reigned 1729–1758), the able ruler who built modern Travancore and dedicated the kingdom to Sree Padmanabha. Through his friendship with Eustachius De Lannoy, the Flemish Catholic officer who served the Maharaja faithfully as head of his army after the battle of Colachel (1741), he came to know Christ, and in 1745 he was baptized by the Jesuit Giovanni Battista Buttari at Vadakkankulam, taking the name Lazarus, in Tamil Devasahayam, “God is my help”.

He lived his new faith openly and treated people of every caste as brothers and sisters. His conversion caused deep opposition among some in the court and in society, and in 1749 he was arrested. After about three years of imprisonment and suffering, he was shot at Kattadimalai near Aralvaimozhy on 14 January 1752. Accounts of the period differ, and the Church's judgment concerns only his faith: she honors him as a martyr who forgave and prayed, and condemns no one. Marthanda Varma is remembered with respect as a great and devout ruler; under him and his successors Christian communities lived and worshipped in Travancore. Devasahayam was beatified at Nagercoil in 2012 and canonized by Pope Francis on 15 May 2022, the first Indian layman to be declared a saint.
The Latin hierarchy of 1886 and the dioceses of Kerala

On 1 September 1886 Pope Leo XIII, with the apostolic letter Humanae salutis auctor, established the regular Catholic hierarchy in India. Verapoly became a metropolitan archdiocese, Quilon a diocese, and in the same year an agreement with Portugal restored Cochin as a Padroado diocese and made Goa a patriarchate. In 1887 the St Thomas Christians in communion with Rome were separated from the Latin jurisdiction into their own vicariates, an important step toward their own hierarchy. In 1934 Joseph Attipetty became the first Indian archbishop of Verapoly.

New Latin dioceses followed as the community grew: Calicut (1923), Kottar and Vijayapuram (1930), Trivandrum (1937), Alleppey (1952), Punalur (1985), Kottapuram (1987), Neyyattinkara (1996), Kannur (1998) and Sultanpet (2013), which serves Tamil- and Malayalam-speaking Latin Catholics in the Palakkad region. Kottar, home of Saint Devasahayam and Xavier's church, now lies in Tamil Nadu. Trivandrum was raised to a metropolitan see in 2004, and Calicut in 2025.
The Latin Church in Kerala today

Today the Latin Church in Kerala has twelve dioceses grouped in three ecclesiastical provinces, under the metropolitan archbishops of Trivandrum, Verapoly and Calicut. Its bishops meet in the Kerala Region Latin Catholic Bishops' Council (KRLCBC), and the Kerala Region Latin Catholic Council (KRLCC), formed in the early 2000s, brings together bishops, clergy, religious and lay leaders as the common voice of the community in Church and society. With the Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara bishops they form the Kerala Catholic Bishops' Council (KCBC); nationally the Latin bishops form the Conference of Catholic Bishops of India (CCBI), and all three Churches together the Catholic Bishops' Conference of India (CBCI).

The Latin Church is the largest of the three Catholic Churches in India as a whole, and in Kerala it is a Church of the coast, the poor and the missions: thousands of its priests and sisters serve across India and the world. Its saints and holy people, Francis Xavier, Devasahayam, Joseph Vaz, Mother Eliswa and many Servants of God whose causes are open, call it to holiness. Its task now is the one Xavier left: to proclaim Christ with courage and love, to stand with the poor of the coast, and to live in communion with the Eastern Catholic Churches and in friendship with all Christians and all neighbors. “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of the messenger who announces peace” (Isaiah 52:7).
notes: The Latin Church is one of the twenty-four Churches sui iuris in the one Catholic Church; in India there are three: the Latin, the Syro-Malabar and the Syro-Malankara. All are equal in dignity and in communion with the Bishop of Rome (Orientalium Ecclesiarum 3; CCEO c. 27).

Dates for the earliest period (John of Montecorvino, Jordanus, Marignolli) come from a few letters and travel accounts; scholars differ on details, and nothing certain is known of the Quilon community after the mid-fourteenth century.

The Synod of Diamper and the Coonan Cross Oath are interpreted differently by the various Churches of Kerala. This lesson gives a brief Catholic account without blaming any community; readers of other traditions may tell the story differently, and their view deserves a respectful hearing.

On Saint Devasahayam: historical sources are limited and partly from Church records written later. The Church's canonization declares his martyrdom for the faith; it is not a judgment on Maharaja Marthanda Varma, whose memory deserves respect, nor on the Hindu people of Travancore.

Please verify recent details locally before teaching: the elevation of Calicut as a metropolitan see (2025), the present number and grouping of Kerala Latin dioceses, the founding year of the KRLCC, and the current status of causes such as that of Mother Eliswa Vakayil (reported beatified in 2025).
Mangalore, Bombay, Goa and other Latin dioceses outside Kerala have their own rich histories; this lesson focuses on Kerala and its neighbors, and does not cover them fully.
